about.title: Brea Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Brea's mix of shopping centers, apartment complexes, and busy retail corridors near Imperial Highway and Lambert Road means plenty of foot traffic across parking lots, entryways, and stairwells. When a property owner or manager lets a spill, broken step, or poor lighting go unaddressed, someone can get hurt. California law requires an injured person to show the owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard and failed to fix it or warn visitors. That's why what happens right after a fall matters: photos of the hazard, witness names, and a request to preserve surveillance footage can make the difference in a claim. LawProactive doesn't practice law or charge fees — we simply connect Brea residents hurt in a fall with an independent attorney who can evaluate the property owner's responsibility and help gather the evidence needed before it disappears.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney Early After a Fall in Brea

items.title: Notice Is Everything
items.desc: California requires proof the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can help track down maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records to establish that notice.

items.title: Surveillance Footage Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many Brea businesses overwrite security video within days or weeks. Getting a preservation letter sent quickly can be the difference between having evidence and losing it.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, Your Claim
items.desc: Even if a property owner argues you weren't watching where you stepped, California's pure comparative fault rule means you may still recover a share of damages tied to their percentage of fault.

items.question: I slipped in a store parking lot in Brea — who's responsible?
items.answer: Responsibility can fall on the property owner, the tenant business, or a maintenance contractor, depending on who controlled the area and who knew about the hazard. An attorney can help sort out which party or parties may be liable. Documentation of the specific spot and condition is important since parking lots change quickly.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in California?
items.answer: Generally you have two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity, such as a city building or public sidewalk in Brea, the deadline is much shorter and requires an earlier formal claim. It's best to have this reviewed as soon as possible.

items.question: What if I didn't take photos right after I fell?
items.answer: It's not ideal, but it's not necessarily fatal to a claim. An attorney can still pursue incident reports, employee statements, maintenance records, and any available video. Acting sooner rather than later gives the best chance of recovering that kind of evidence before it's lost.
